messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Miguel is a twenty-two-year-old HVAC technician from a close-knit Latin American family, and for the past fourteen months he has been living in a state he does not recognise as his own. The accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late July, when he was on a rooftop performing a routine compressor replacement for a commercial building. His coworker, an older man named Raúl, was on the ground handing up tools. Miguel had the new compressor balanced on the dolly when his grip slipped—his gloves were slick with condensation, or maybe his hand just cramped, he would replay that microsecond a thousand times—and the two-hundred-pound unit tipped over the edge. He heard Raúl shout, then a wet, heavy sound, then a silence that lasted less than a second before the screaming started. The air filled with the sharp, sweet-chemical smell of refrigerant mixed with something metallic and coppery. Raúl survived, but his pelvis was shattered and he spent six weeks in the ICU. Miguel visited him once in the hospital. He could not look at Raúl’s wife. He has not visited again.

In the weeks afterward, Miguel could not stop going over the details. He sat on his couch for hours, replaying the identical sequence: the dolly, the tilt, the weight, his hand. He searched for the exact moment he could have done something different—tied a safety rope, waited for help, tightened his grip. Every version ended the same way, but he kept searching. He began to feel that the memory itself was not his own; it was like watching a video of someone else making a mistake, except that someone was also him. Sometimes, without warning, the smell would come back. He would be standing in a client’s basement or driving his van, and suddenly the air would go chemical and coppery, and his heart would slam against his ribs, his palms would soak, and he would have to pull over and wait for it to pass. His body had become a traitor. He could no longer trust his hands, his reflexes, his judgment. He was certain that at any moment he could do something catastrophic again.

Silence became a poison. In the quiet between HVAC cycles, in the stillness of his apartment at night, he would freeze, listening for the sound that meant something terrible was about to happen. He learned to keep noise on—television, music, a fan—but even then his muscles stayed tight. He started refusing service calls that felt stressful: anything with a tight deadline, a difficult customer, an unfamiliar rooftop. Then he started calling in sick on days that reminded him of the accident—the anniversary itself, the day Raúl was discharged, the day he first went back to work after the accident. His supervisor noticed. Miguel was given a warning. He quit before they could fire him, telling himself he needed a break. That was eight months ago. Now he lives off savings and the occasional under-the-table repair for neighbors, but only in the apartment complex where he rents, because that is the only place he feels even close to safe. He does not drive his van anymore.

The person he used to be—a reliable young man who helped his mother with the bills, who played soccer on weekends, who laughed easily with his cousins—feels like a stranger. Miguel looks in the mirror and sees someone hollow-eyed and jumpy, someone who cannot forgive himself for not doing more. In his worst moments he replays the scene and imagines himself reaching out and catching the compressor, or shouting a warning a second earlier, and the guilt is a physical weight on his chest. He has begun to believe that he does not deserve to feel safe, that the constant vigilance is a kind of punishment he has earned.

Two weeks ago, his mother found him sitting in the dark at four in the morning, staring at the wall, a fan blowing directly on his face. She made an appointment at the community mental health clinic and told him she would drive him there herself. Miguel agreed because he could not find a reason to say no. He is afraid of what the therapist will think of him, afraid that telling the story out loud will make it more real, but he is more afraid of another night like that one, waiting for a silence that is never really silent.
